content.text: Students continue tracing how Greek monsters and supernatural encounters shape Percy’s world and identity.
Myths often turn danger into story, and monsters can symbolize fears, consequences, or parts of the past that follow a character.
This lesson prepares students for Lesson 18, when Percy faces a more deceptive danger in the Medusa episode.
Students will need to explain how a challenge raises the stakes in a quest and how modern retellings transform mythic ideas for new audiences.

Partner Reading & Discussion
Directions:

As you reread the key moments with your partner, pay attention to two things: what Percy decides under pressure and what happens because of that decision. Mark one moment when the danger gets worse and one moment when Percy acts like a leader.
When the bus-fight danger becomes clear, what choice does Percy make, and what immediate consequence follows?

Pulse Check
Which statement best explains how the bus fight raises the stakes of Percy’s quest?
It shows that Percy can no longer separate ordinary travel from supernatural danger, so the quest becomes riskier for everyone with him.

Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the question.
Ask:
Why do you think heroes are often tested at the beginning of a quest or journey?

I think that stories test the hero right away so that readers can see whether the hero is truly ready for his quest. An early challenge shows what the hero still needs to learn and raises the pressure fast.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Today we will track Percy’s split-second choices during the bus fight and compare how the novel and film develop a feeling of tension.
Teacher Tip

The Chapter 10 bus scene includes fantasy violence, panic, and danger on public transportation. Before reading, remind students that this is fantasy conflict, not behavior to copy, and keep the discussion grounded in how authors build tension and character development rather than in personal experiences with danger.
Activate the connection between the prophecy in Lesson 16 and Percy’s first major obstacle on the road.

Use this part of the lesson to remind students to pause when they come across an unfamiliar word. Remind students that effective readers use context clues, punctuation and word parts to figure out the meaning of words. Then if they are still unsure or want to verify their definition, they can check the meaning in a dictionary or online vocabulary resource.
Context Clues
Target words: submit, impulsive
Say:

In a fast‑moving scene, the author doesn’t stop to explain every word. Instead, we have to use story context, clues around the unfamiliar word, and even punctuation to infer what’s really happening. Building this skill helps us uncover the deeper meaning of a scene, not just follow the action.
Display the following sentence from Chapter 10:
“Submit now,” she hissed. “And you will not suffer eternal torment.” (p. 165)
Teach: Using context to infer meaning
Say:

When I come across a word I don’t know, or used in a way that doesn’t make sense with the meaning I know, I don’t pull it out of the scene and study it on its own. I look closely at what’s happening around it and ask myself what kind of word would make sense in that moment. When Mrs. Dodds says “
Submit

now,” in a hiss, it definitely sounds like a threat. She is not talking about submitting homework. If characters are trapped, scared, or being forced to obey, the word submit in this context probably means “to give in” or “go along with.” When I replace "submit”
with “to give in,” it fits the situation and makes sense within the context, and also I see a connection to ‘
submit
’ in the sense of handing in an assignment, which was the meaning I was already familiar with.
Ask:
In the moment when Percy and the others realize the bus may stop and they cannot simply escape, what clues can help you infer the meaning of
submit
The clues show that someone is being pressured to obey. Because the characters are cornered and the danger is getting closer, submit most likely means to give in or do what the other side wants.
Display the following sentence from Chapter 10.
“What I did next was so impulsive and dangerous I should’ve been named ADHD poster child of the year.” (p. 164)
Prompt students to turn and talk with a partner to respond to the following question:
Ask:
Percy reacts before he fully thinks things through. What does the context tell you about the meaning of the word
impulsive
in this scene?

In this scene, impulsive means acting very fast without taking much time to think about the outcomes. The danger is so sudden that Percy moves quickly, which can help him but can also create new problems.

The prefix sub helped me with submit, and the base pulse helped me remember i

Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now that we have practiced using clues from an action-packed scene to understand the deeper meaning, we are ready to track how Percy’s decisions and their consequences build tension in the chapter.
Support students in using scene-based clues and causal language to infer word meaning and connect vocabulary to Percy’s actions under pressure.
Language Focus:
Context clue language
Causal connectors
Precise action verbs
Before Activity
Invite students to orally complete this frame with a partner: “The clue that helped me most was ___ because ___.”
Prompt students to name the exact clue, not just the word they guessed from.
If students give a broad definition, push for a scene-specific meaning by asking how the word works in this bus-fight moment.
You said “He just did it fast”—we can explain that by saying, “He acted impulsively because the danger gave him almost no time to think.”
That idea connects to submit because the scene shows pressure to obey, not just a random action.
The clue that helped me infer ___ was ___.
In this scene, ___ probably means ___ because ___.
This word matters because it shows Percy is ___ under pressure.
Allow students to briefly test a word meaning in a shared home language, if helpful, before restating it in English.
Invite students to compare prefixes they know across languages when helpful.
If students confuse a word’s general meaning with its scene-specific meaning → Prompt: “What does the situation add to the meaning here?”
If students name a definition without evidence → Prompt: “Point to the exact detail or punctuation mark that helped you make that inference.”
Student cites a nearby clue and uses it to infer a reasonable meaning.
Student revises an informal explanation into a more precise academic explanation with because or so.

Struggling with: Using Scene Clues to Infer Meaning

Direct students to underline one exact detail before they say a definition. Moving from Everyday Language to Academic Language: Offer the frame “In this scene, ___ means ___ because ___.” Written Output: Allow students to give an oral response or use speech-to-text for their Personal Dictionary explanation.
Ready for extension

Ask students to compare impulsive and heroic and explain how a quick action can be both helpful and risky. Ask students to identify a second word in the scene whose meaning becomes clearer because of the same context clues.

Part A: Track Decisions and Consequences (
The Lightning Thief
, Chapter 10, pp. 158–167) (RL.6.5) (15 minutes)
Partner Reading & Discussion

In this part of the lesson, students look closely at how rising danger shapes Percy’s choices. You’ll guide them to notice when the threat intensifies and when Percy steps into a leadership role. This framing helps them connect conflict, decision, and consequence as the scene unfolds.
Have partners reread key moments in the text: when the old women appear threatening, when Percy realizes the riders are trapped, and when he acts.
Say these Directions:

As you reread the key moments with your partner, pay attention to two things: what Percy decides under pressure and what happens because of that decision. Mark one moment when the danger gets worse and one moment when Percy acts like a leader.
Teach: Analyzing decisions and consequences.
Say:

When we analyze a character’s actions and decisions, we need to understand the circumstances that lead to the decision and the impact that follows. An effective analysis clearly describes the conflict the character faces, the decision they make, and the consequences of that decision—and explains how all three are connected.
Ask:
When the bus-fight danger becomes clear, what choice does Percy make, and what immediate consequence follows?

When Percy realizes the Furies are attacking, he stops just reacting and starts protecting the group. The immediate consequence is that the fight becomes public and chaotic, which shows the quest is now dangerous even in ordinary places like a bus.
Ask:
In what ways does the encounter with the Furies show that monsters are often symbols of a character’s past?

The Furies connect Percy’s current quest to earlier trouble because they are not a brand-new danger. They remind readers of the museum attack and of the way Percy’s life keeps getting interrupted by forces he cannot escape. That makes them feel like the past is following him into the present.
Ask:
How does this episode serve as one challenge in a growing series of obstacles?

This episode is not the whole quest by itself. It works like the next link in a chain because Percy has already received the prophecy, and now the road itself becomes unsafe. The challenge pushes the plot forward by showing that the journey will include repeated tests, not just one battle.
Pulse Check (RL.6.5)
Which statement best explains the connection between the bus fight and Percy’s larger quest?
A. It shows that Percy can no longer separate ordinary travel from supernatural danger, so the quest becomes riskier for everyone with him
Correct: This answer explains both the event and its effect on the larger quest. The bus fight shows that monsters can attack in everyday spaces and that Percy’s choices affect the whole group.
B. It mainly slows the story down so the reader can get a break after the prophecy.
Incorrect: A student might choose this if they focus only on the pause in travel, but the scene actually increases danger and pressure.
C. It proves Percy has already mastered every skill he will need for the quest.
Incorrect: A student might choose this if they notice Percy acting quickly, but the scene shows developing leadership, not complete mastery.
D. It matters only because it introduces a new vehicle and setting for the story.
Incorrect: A student might focus on the setting change, but the real importance is how the encounter escalates the quest and Percy’s responsibilities.
Support students in evaluating Percy’s decisions with extended explanations that connect action, consequence, and character development.
Language Focus:
Causal language
Sequence language
Evaluative verbs
Before Activity
Have students rehearse one sentence aloud using this pattern: “Percy decides to ___, which leads to ___.”
Encourage students to move past one-word judgments like brave or reckless by asking what pressure shaped Percy’s action.
Prompt students to build on a partner’s comment using the unit discussion moves rather than starting over with a separate idea.
You said “He had to do something”—we can say, “He acts under pressure because waiting would put the group in greater danger.”
You said “It gets worse”—we can say, “The consequence raises the stakes because danger now follows Percy into public spaces.”
Percy chooses to ___ because ___.
One consequence of that choice is ___, which raises the stakes because ___.
Building on that idea, this challenge reveals ___ about Percy as a hero.
Invite students to rehearse with a partner in the language they use most comfortably and then restate the idea in English using the provided frame.
Validate brief first drafts of thinking and help students expand them into fuller academic sentences.
If students retell the fight without naming the choice → Prompt: “Where is the exact decision point in the scene?”
If students judge Percy as simply right or wrong → Prompt: “What pressure shaped his choice, and what alternatives did he actually have?”
Student explains a decision using because, so, or which leads to.
Student distinguishes between the event itself and the larger consequence for the quest.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Identifying the Decision Point

Direct them to the exact moment Percy shifts from noticing danger to acting. Explaining Stakes: Offer the frame “This matters for the quest because now ___.” Processing the Scene in Writing: Allow students to bullet the pressure, choice, and consequence before speaking or writing in sentences.
Ready for extension

Ask students to compare this obstacle with the museum attack and explain what has changed in Percy’s response. Ask students to argue whether the scene shows more growth in Percy’s courage or in his leadership, using two details.
Part B: Novel vs. Film (RL.6.7) (15 minutes)
Think-Pair-Share

In this part of the lesson, students compare how the novel and the film shape the bus‑fight scene. The goal is to help them notice how each medium creates mood and shows characters’ responses, and how those choices affect our understanding of the consequences. This sets them up to use the T‑Chart and discuss their observations with a partner.
Say these Directions:
We are going to compare the bus fight scene in both the novel and the film. Consider the following question to support your comparison.
Ask:
How do the text and the movie each portray the mood of the scene, the characters’ responses, and the consequences of those responses?

In the left column of the T-Chart, record what the novel helps you notice and in the right column, record what the film helps you notice. After recording your notes, share them with a partner. Add one idea to your partner’s thinking using one of these phrases: “I would like to add . . . ,” “Building on that idea . . . ,” or “One way this connects is . . .”

Prompt students to reread the bus fight scene and discuss the question with a partner. Direct students to record how the text conveys the mood of the scene, the characters’ responses, and the consequences of those responses in the left column of the T-Chart.

Then, show the teacher-selected bus-fight clip once without stopping. Then, show it a second time. Direct students to record how the film conveys the mood of the scene, the characters’ responses, and the consequences of those responses in the right column of the T-Chart.
Teach: Comparing stories in different mediums
Say:

When I compare a novel to a film, I ask what each version makes easiest to notice. The novel gives me Percy’s inner perspective and the narrator’s tone, while the film gives me faces, sound, speed, and camera choices. If one version feels more personal and another feels more explosive, that difference matters. Together, the book and the film help me understand the challenges Percy faces and how he is growing into a leader in response to those events.
Ask:
What emotion feels strongest in the novel version of the bus fight, and what detail helps create it?
In the novel, confusion mixed with urgency feels strongest. Percy’s first-person narration makes the danger feel personal because we stay close to what he notices and how fast he has to react.
Ask:
What emotion or mood feels strongest in the film version, and what visual or sound choice creates it?
In the film, the tone feels louder and more dramatic. Fast movement, intense sound, and the actors’ facial expressions make the attack feel more explosive than it does on the written page.
Ask:
How does the film change the way we see Percy making decisions under pressure?

The film makes Percy look more visibly action-ready, while the novel lets us understand more of his confusion from the inside. Because of that, the film emphasizes fast hero action, whereas the book emphasizes pressure building inside Percy’s point of view.
Reflection (RL.6.7)
Reflect on your understanding using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to compare different versions of the same story?
Support students in using comparative and collaborative language to explain how the novel and film portray emotion, tone, and high-pressure decisions differently.
Language Focus:
Comparative transitions
Media-analysis language
Collaborative discussion stems
Before Activity
Invite students to orally rehearse one comparison using this stem: “In the novel ___, whereas in the film ___.”
Prompt students to name a specific film choice such as sound, facial expression, movement, or pacing instead of saying only the movie “shows more.”
Model how to build on a classmate’s idea so discussion becomes cumulative, not a series of isolated comments.
You said, “The movie is more intense”—we can say, “The film creates a more intense tone through faster pacing, striking visuals, and louder sound.”
You said, “The book tells more”—we can say, “The novel gives readers more access to Percy’s inner thoughts, perspective and narrator tone.”
In the novel, the scene feels ___ because ___.
In contrast, the film emphasizes ___ through ___.
Building on that idea, one way this connects is ___.
Encourage partners to orally test a comparison before writing it into the T-Chart.
Treat students’ noticing of facial expressions, movement, and sound as valid analytical entry points into media comparison.
If students summarize the clip without comparing it to the text → Prompt: “What does the film emphasize that the novel emphasizes differently?”
If students confuse Percy’s narrator tone with the tone of the whole scene → Prompt: “Which part comes from Percy’s voice, and which part comes from the overall mood?”
Student uses a comparative word such as whereas, unlike, or in contrast.
Student names one specific media feature and connects it to emotion or tone.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Comparing Instead of Retelling

Give the frame: “Both versions show ___, but the novel ___, while the film ___.” Naming Media Features: Offer a small bank of choices: sound, pacing, facial expression, camera focus, movement. Written Expression: Allow students to orally record their comparison before turning it into one written sentence.
Ready for extension

Ask students to explain which version better emphasizes Percy’s leadership and defend that claim with two supporting details. Ask students to analyze what is gained and what is lost when the scene shifts from Percy’s narration to a visual medium.
Part A: Track Decisions and Consequences (RL.6.5)
Students will analyze how Percy’s choices during the bus fight raise the stakes of the quest.
Part B: Novel vs. Film Pressure Test (RL.6.7)
Students will compare how the novel and film show emotions, mood, and decision-making under pressure.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:

Write three to five sentences explaining how the bus fight raises the stakes of Percy’s quest and how both the text and film versions convey the tension in this scene. Use at least two specific details—one from the novel and one from the film.
Ask:
How does this challenge help readers understand Percy’s development as a hero?

The bus fight raises the stakes because Percy learns that monsters can attack him even in ordinary places, not just at camp or in school. In the novel, his first-person narration shows how confused and pressured he feels as he tries to protect the group. In contrast, the film uses fast action and sound to make the danger feel more real and explosive. Together, both versions show Percy becoming more heroic because he starts making choices that protect others even when he is scared.
Performance Task Bridge
Say:

Today, you practiced one of the key skills you’ll need for the performance task. You explained how a challenge changes a quest and used evidence to compare two versions of the same scene. This kind of explanation will help you show how modern texts build on and reshape mythic ideas.
Ask:
Which tool helped you most today: tracking consequence, using a comparison word, or noticing a film choice?
Tracking consequence helped me most because it moved me past summary and helped me explain why the scene matters for the whole quest.
Students will write a short evidence-based comparison explaining how the bus fight is portrayed in both the text and film..
Have students access their copy of
The Lightning Thief
. Instruct students to:
Read the summary of Chapter 11, pp. 168–top of 178 ending with “. . . into the garden of statues.”
Read and annotate
The Lightning Thief
Chapter 10, pp. 178–187, beginning with “Aunty Em directed us . . .” and ending at p. 187.
Teacher Tip

For homework, students will move toward the Medusa episode. Before assigning it, flag that Percy’s narration includes a harmful stereotype when he assumes information about a veiled woman based only on appearance. Remind students to read critically: Percy is a character in a book with limited understanding, and readers are responsible for questioning assumptions rather than accepting them.

standards.description: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word’s position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

Compare and contrast the experience of reading a story, drama, or poem to listening to or viewing an audio, video, or live version of the text, including contrasting what they “see” and “hear” when reading the text to what they perceive when they listen or watch.

Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
Describe how a particular story’s or drama’s plot unfolds in a series of episodes as well as how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution.
Analyze how a particular sentence, chapter, scene, or stanza fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the theme, setting, or plot.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with light support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with substantial support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with moderate support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language resources to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the specific language used to present ideas and claims that are well supported and distinguishing them from those that are not), with light support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use language to support ideas and arguments with detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the precise vocabulary used to present evidence, or the phrasing used to signal a shift in meaning), with substantial support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., showing the clarity of the phrasing used to present an argument), with moderate support.

Expand sentences with a variety of adverbials (e.g., adverbs, adverb phrases and clauses, prepositional phrases) to provide details (e.g., time, manner, place, cause) about a variety of familiar and new activities and processes.
Expand sentences with simple adverbials (e.g., adverbs, adverb phrases, prepositional phrases) to provide details (e.g., time, manner, place, cause) about a familiar activity or process.

Expand sentences with an increasing variety of adverbials (e.g., adverbs, adverb phrases, prepositional phrases) to provide details (e.g., time, manner, place, cause) about a familiar or new activity or process.
